pamphlet_excerpts: Orienteering First Aid: Orienteering is a physically demanding activity that takes place over several kilometers of very mixed and often rugged terrain (p. 66).
Orienteering First Aid Principle 2: Hot weather may result in sunburn, heatstroke, heat exhaustion, and dehydration, while cold weather can lead to hypothermia and dehydration (p. 66).
Orienteering First Aid Principle 3: In the hurry to be first, you might stumble onto dangerous animals or poisonous plants (p. 66).
Orienteering First Aid Principle 4: Before going out, spend a fewminutes reviewing possible injuries and their treatment (p. 66).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Orienteering First Aid): The best thing you can do to prevent injury is to be well-rested, well-fed, and physically fit before going out on an orienteeringcourse (p. 66).
Step 2 (Orienteering First Aid): A normal night's sleep and healthy meals will help you endure the rigors of the course and decrease the possibility of a physical or mental slip (p. 66).
Step 3 (Orienteering First Aid): If you are not physically fit, you may be particularly vulnerable to heat (p. 66).
Step 4 (Orienteering First Aid): Dehydration is caused by lack of water in the body (p. 66).

quiz_item.question: When taking a bearing from a topographic map in an area with a 12-degree west magnetic declination, why must you account for declination before following your compass in the field?
options: A. Because contour lines on a topographic map shift position seasonally as soil moisture changes.
B. Because a baseplate compass needle always points toward the geographic North Pole rather than magnetic north.
C. Because map grid lines align with true north while the compass needle points to magnetic north, and ignoring a 12-degree difference will pull you far off course over distance.
D. Because metal control flags placed at orienteering checkpoints reverse the polarity of the compass housing.
choices: A. Because contour lines on a topographic map shift position seasonally as soil moisture changes.
B. Because a baseplate compass needle always points toward the geographic North Pole rather than magnetic north.
C. Because map grid lines align with true north while the compass needle points to magnetic north, and ignoring a 12-degree difference will pull you far off course over distance.

quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Because map grid lines align with true north while the compass needle points to magnetic north, and ignoring a 12-degree difference will pull you far off course over distance.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Magnetic declination is the angular difference between true north (shown on the map) and magnetic north (where the compass needle points); failing to adjust for it causes significant navigation errors.

pamphlet_excerpts: Map Symbols and Topographic Features: Using a Topographic Map. maps you will find a number on it that tells its elevation abovesea level (p. 14).

Map Symbols and Topographic Features Principle 2: On orienteering maps, the index contour line does not have an elevation number, but is thicker than the others and is used as a guide for the eye (p. 14).
Map Symbols and Topographic Features Principle 3: You can also "see" the shape of the terrain from the profile of the lines on the paper (p. 14).
Map Symbols and Topographic Features Principle 4: If a mountain is perfectly conical like a wizard's hat, the contour lines depicting the mountain will look like a bull's-eye (p. 14).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Map Symbols and Topographic Features): Each contour line will be perfectly circular, and all will be the same distance apart (p. 14).
Step 2 (Map Symbols and Topographic Features): At one part of the mountain, the contour line may intersect a valley or a depression (p. 14).
Step 3 (Map Symbols and Topographic Features): If the contour line ran into the valley, it would lose elevation and would no longer be considered the same contour line (p. 14).
Step 4 (Map Symbols and Topographic Features): When a higher point like a ridge is encountered, the contour line will "V" downward (p. 14).

Teach orienteering techniques to your patrol Principle 2: Beginners' courses rely heavily on handrails to help the novice get to each control (p. 41).
Teach orienteering techniques to your patrol Principle 3: The route for the easiest courses may actually go right down a trail or road, the handrail (p. 41).

Teach orienteering techniques to your patrol Principle 4: Collecting, Check-Off, and Catching Features Always look around and take note of the features you pass as you move toward the next control (p. 41).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Teach orienteering techniques to your patrol): There may be some obvious features along the route, such as a large pond or small lake, that will help send you in the right direction (p. 41).
Step 2 (Teach orienteering techniques to your patrol): These are collecting features, which lie between you and the control (p. 41).
Step 3 (Teach orienteering techniques to your patrol): Equally important but less obvious are check-off features, which you will see along the way (p. 41).
